title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 53–54
description: Carefully selected upper-intermediate vocabulary for periods of time, punctuality, duration, physical dimensions, measurement and changes in size.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study from the user-supplied book. Vocabulary targets follow the source topics and relevant exercise vocabulary; teaching examples and explanatory notes are newly written. Original exercise texts, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Teaching pages, timing contrasts, dimension collocations, illustrations, usage boxes, exercises 53.1–53.4 and 54.1–54.5, and relevant answer-key entries were checked for vocabulary, grammar, prepositions and register.
audit.pronunciation: British English phonemic guidance given when reliable; longer expressions and uncertain variants omit IPA. Pronounceable targets are used for word audio, with complete sentences reserved for example audio.
audit.languagePolicy: All fields use English except Brazilian Portuguese translations under pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Reviewed the supplied teaching and exercise pages alongside the answer key; checked meaning, collocations, contrastive usage, prepositions, natural original examples, stable IDs and static Word/Sentence audio fields against the canonical reference structure. Static structural validation was performed. No live app import, browser TTS or speech-recognition test was performed.
audit.limitations: Empty audio values indicate that no recording is bundled; browser TTS and recogniser accuracy depend on implementation and voice. Actual app import and live playback have not been tested.

units.title: Unit 53 — Time
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 112–113 (PDF pages 113–114).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Distinguish historical ages, eras, periods, spells, stages and phases by context.
Use time phrases precisely, especially in time versus on time and by the time followed by a present tense clause.
Differentiate neutral and negative ways of talking about time passing and events continuing.
Choose natural adjectives for brief duration and timeless qualities.

sectionsChecked: A: Periods of time and typical contexts
B: Useful expressions with time; in time and on time contrast
D: Adjectives of duration and common mistakes

items.example: We live in an age when information travels instantly.
items.note: An extended historical period; often used in names such as the Stone Age.

items.example: Scientists study evidence left by the last Ice Age.
items.note: A geological period associated with extensive glaciation.

items.example: The museum displays tools made during the Stone Age.
items.note: The name of a major prehistoric period.

items.example: Many castles in the region date from the Middle Ages.
items.note: A named historical period; always plural in this expression.

items.pt: era da computação; era dos computadores
items.example: Privacy has become an important concern in the computer age.
items.note: A historical age can be named after a defining technology or activity.

items.example: The agreement marked the start of a new era in international relations.
items.note: Often refers to an extended period characterised by particular events or conditions.

items.example: There will be a six-month period for public consultation.
items.note: A general term for a length of time; may have a defined beginning and end.

items.example: A brief spell of cold weather delayed the outdoor work.
items.note: An indefinite, often relatively short period; common with weather or illness.

items.example: The prototype is now at the final stage of testing.
items.note: One identifiable step in a process or course of development.

items.example: The team is entering a new phase of the research programme.
items.note: A period forming part of a longer process; sometimes interchangeable with stage.

items.example: My brother went through a phase of reading detective novels every night.
items.note: Use go through a phase of followed by a noun or an -ing form.

items.example: The design is still at an early stage of development.
items.note: A common combination for describing progress through successive steps.

items.pt: por algum tempo; durante um período
items.example: For a time, I worked mainly on embedded firmware.
items.note: For an unspecified period, usually in the past.

items.example: Keep the older controller in service for the time being.
items.note: Means for now, while the current situation lasts; not a specified duration.

items.example: Debugging an intermittent fault can be frustrating at times.
items.note: Means occasionally; can appear at the beginning or end of a sentence.

items.pt: quando; até o momento em que
items.example: By the time the visitors arrive, the equipment will be ready.
items.note: In future-time clauses, use present tense after by the time, not will.

items.example: We review the calibration procedure from time to time.
items.note: Something happens occasionally, not regularly or frequently.

items.example: Please connect the sensors one at a time during the test.
items.note: Refers to handling people or things individually rather than together.

items.example: We reached the platform in time to catch the last train.
items.note: Means early enough for an event or action; contrast with punctual on time.

items.example: The morning train arrived on time despite the heavy rain.
items.note: Means at the scheduled time, neither early nor late; contrast with in time.

items.pt: repetidas vezes; muitas e muitas vezes
items.example: I have reminded the team time and time again to save their changes.
items.note: Emphatic repetition, often used when expressing annoyance.

items.pt: ao longo de; durante o decorrer de
items.example: Over the course of the project, we discovered several design limitations.
items.note: Used for change or developments across a span of time, particularly a long period.

items.example: Several months elapsed between the two interviews.
items.note: Formal verb for time passing; often used in past or perfect forms.

items.pt: o tempo voa; o tempo passa depressa
items.example: Time flies when I am absorbed in a difficult engineering problem.
items.note: Informal expression meaning that time seems to pass quickly.

items.example: The introductory course lasted for four weeks.
items.note: A verb expressing how long an event or state continues.

items.example: The discussion went on longer than anyone expected.
items.note: Used here of an activity continuing over time, sometimes for longer than desired.

items.example: The negotiations dragged on without a clear decision.
items.note: Suggests that something continues tediously or longer than wanted; stronger than go on.

items.example: A momentary interruption in the signal did not affect the results.
items.note: Describes something lasting only a very short moment.

items.example: She had only a fleeting chance to speak to the guest lecturer.
items.note: Very brief and quickly passing; often used with glimpse or moment.

items.example: Through the crowd, I caught a fleeting glimpse of the actor.
items.note: An especially short or incomplete look at someone or something.

items.pt: atemporal; que não perde a atualidade
items.example: The architect aimed for a timeless design rather than a short-lived trend.
items.note: Describes something that does not seem tied to a particular time or fashion.

units.title: Unit 54 — Distances and dimensions
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 114–115 (PDF pages 115–116).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose wide or broad and tall or high using natural collocations, and state physical dimensions correctly.
Develop noun and verb families for length, width, breadth, height, distance and depth.
Contrast verbs for lengthening, broadening, expanding, contracting, shrinking and extending.
Use fixed distance-preposition patterns and distinguish abstract from physical meanings.

sectionsChecked: A: Wide and broad; tall and high; dimension order
B: Deep and shallow; swimming-pool illustration
C: Word families, collocations, distance compounds and opposites
D: Verbs expressing changes in dimensions

items.section: A · Broad, wide, tall and high
items.example: The workshop has a wide entrance for moving large machines.
items.note: The usual adjective for the width of roads, rooms and physical objects.

items.section: A · Broad, wide, tall and high
items.example: Safety engineering is a broad field involving many disciplines.
items.note: Often used for large scope or expanse; wide is more usual for a road or room.

items.section: A · Broad, wide, tall and high
items.example: Beyond the village there was a broad expanse of open grassland.
items.note: A natural combination for a large continuous area of land.

items.section: A · Broad, wide, tall and high
items.example: The laboratory owns a wide range of diagnostic instruments.
items.note: Range often takes wide or broad when many different options exist.

items.section: A · Broad, wide, tall and high
items.example: This specialist supplier sells only a narrow range of components.
items.note: Opposite of a broad or wide range of options.

items.section: A · Broad, wide, tall and high
items.example: A tall tree shades the front of the house.
items.note: Used for people and things that are high and relatively narrow, such as trees.

items.section: A · Broad, wide, tall and high
items.example: The path crosses a high mountain pass.
items.note: More usual than tall for mountains, walls and other elevated things.

items.section: A · Broad, wide, tall and high
items.example: The new cable is ten metres long.
items.note: Dimension adjectives follow measurements: ten metres long, four metres wide.

items.section: A · Broad, wide, tall and high
items.example: The office is six metres long and four metres wide.
items.note: Put the measurement before the adjective: six metres long, four metres wide.

items.example: The reservoir is deepest near the dam.
items.note: Opposite of shallow; commonly used of water, holes or containers.

items.example: Young children should stay in the shallow part of the pool.
items.note: Opposite of deep, especially for water or a container.

items.example: The swimming instructor asked beginners to avoid the deep end.
items.note: The part of a swimming pool with greater water depth.

items.example: The youngest learners practised in the shallow end.
items.note: The area of a pool where the water is less deep.

items.example: Check the length of the cable before cutting it.
items.note: Noun corresponding to long; do not confuse it with width.

items.pt: uma travessia do comprimento da piscina
items.example: She completed twenty lengths of the pool during training.
items.note: One full journey from one end of a swimming pool to the other.

items.example: We need to lengthen the cable to reach the far socket.
items.note: To make or become longer; contrast with shorten.

items.example: Obtaining permission involved a lengthy approval process.
items.note: Often refers to duration and may imply an inconveniently long time.

items.example: She often makes long-distance journeys for work.
items.note: Compound adjective used before nouns such as call, journey or driver.

items.example: The new route should shorten the journey considerably.
items.note: To reduce length or duration; the opposite of lengthen.

items.example: We found a shortcut through the park to the station.
items.note: A shorter route that saves time or distance.

items.example: We measured the width of the table before ordering the cover.
items.note: Noun corresponding to wide.

items.example: The local council plans to widen the narrow bridge.
items.note: To make physically wider; compare broaden for abstract scope.

items.example: Working with another research group could broaden our experience.
items.note: Common with experience, knowledge, opportunities and perspectives.

items.example: A broad-minded manager listens to unconventional suggestions.
items.note: Willing to consider different beliefs and behaviour; opposite of narrow-minded.

items.example: A narrow-minded attitude can prevent a team from exploring new solutions.
items.note: Unwilling to consider unfamiliar ideas or different ways of life.

items.example: Her breadth of technical knowledge impressed the interview panel.
items.note: Noun corresponding to broad; often used for knowledge or experience.

items.example: The height of the ceiling is nearly four metres.
items.note: Noun corresponding to high and tall.

items.example: The sudden silence heightened the audience’s anxiety.
items.note: Common with feelings or emotions rather than physical height.

items.example: Please lower the microphone before the next speaker begins.
items.note: Verb meaning make lower or move down; contrast with raise.

items.example: Raise your hand if you need help with the equipment.
items.note: Verb meaning move or lift upwards; opposite of lower.

items.example: He dreams of visiting faraway islands one day.
items.note: An adjective for places a long way away; often used before a noun.

items.example: The signal originated from a distant monitoring station.
items.note: Describes physical or sometimes emotional distance.

items.example: The distance from our office to the station is about a kilometre.
items.note: A measurable separation between places or objects; patterns include distance from ... to ... and distance between ... and ....

items.example: We recorded the depth of the lake at several points.
items.note: Noun corresponding to deep.

items.example: The unexpected news deepened their sense of uncertainty.
items.note: Often used figuratively with feelings; also possible with physical depth.

items.example: The farmland stretches all the way to the forest.
items.note: For land or objects extending over an area or distance.

items.example: The library will extend its opening hours during exam week.
items.note: To make something longer or larger in space, time or scope.

items.example: As the city spread, new houses appeared beyond the ring road.
items.note: To cover a wider area; unlike expand, often highlights movement across space.

items.example: My wool jumper shrank after I washed it in hot water.
items.note: To become smaller; irregular past shrank or shrunk, participle shrunk.

items.example: The company expanded rapidly after entering new markets.
items.note: To become larger in size or scale; contrast with contract.

items.example: The manufacturing sector contracted during the downturn.
items.note: Formal verb for becoming smaller; the verb is stressed on the second syllable.

items.example: The warning sign is visible at a distance of fifty metres.
items.note: Use at a distance of plus a measurement.

items.example: We could just make out the lighthouse in the distance.
items.note: Something is far away but still visible or audible.

items.example: From a distance, the two buildings look identical.
items.note: Used when viewing or considering something from far away.
